item.title: Italy October services PMI 52.0 vs 51.5 expected
item.description:
• Prior 51.7
  • Composite PMI 50.8 vs 50.8 expected
  • Prior 51.0

Key findings:

  • Growth in activity back in line with trend, supported by stronger new business inflows
  • Business sentiment strongest since November last year
  • Input cost inflation surges to almost four-year high

Comment:

Eleanor Dennison, Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence:

"The Italian service sector maintained its steady path of growth in October, even signalling stronger inflows of new work. The headline reading was back in line with its average trend, having crept higher over the month. "Granular sub-sector data revealed the commercial & professional services segment was the only drag, with the consumer services and software & communication sectors recording fresh upturns. The financials & real estate segment continued to lead growth, despite softening again. "The main challenges facing Italian service companies were softness in export demand and the build-up of cost pressures, two factors that are highly exposed to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Panellists often reported paying more for fuel and energy-related products in their reports, pushing the overall reading for input price inflation to one of its highest since the 2022 energy crisis. Transportation firms are struggling in particular with respect to costs, having signalled one of the strongest increases on record."Keep in mind that the Italian PMIs are never a market-moving release despite Italy being the third largest economy in the Eurozone. They do provide more information about economic activity in the euro area, though. 

As it stands, economic growth remains resilient in the Eurozone and inflationary pressure continue to build amid elevated energy prices caused by the US-Iran war. Everything hinges on the war. The ECB cannot fix an oil supply problem, but it can dampen demand through higher interest rates. The problem is that at some point, higher interest rates and elevated energy prices start putting a strong downward pressure on the economy. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why the Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections is driving gold higher and what to watch next
item.description:
Gold has been rallying strongly this morning as a blue sweep in the US midterm elections became a reality.

As mentioned yesterday, a Democratic congress is going to restrict further tax cuts, defence spending and fiscal expansion in general. This is positive for gold because it’s going to limit the rise in Treasury yields and the US dollar on lower rate hike expectations.

It could also support gold in case Trump decides to escalate the war with Iran as inflation expectations would rise alongside weakening growth outlook, creating a stagflationary environment.

Looking ahead, we have the US NFP report on Friday but it’s unlikely to change much for the Fed unless we see a jump in wage growth or surprisingly weak data. The focus will likely remain on US-Iran negotiations, but at this point, it looks like both an escalation and a de-escalation would provide support gold.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) is approaching the major downward trendline. We can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to target a break below the major upward trendline. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the 4,700 level next, with the 4,500 level as the first target.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we now have a minor upward trendline defining the bullish momentum. If we get a pullback, we can expect the buyers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep targeting a break above the downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets and target a break below the major upward trendline.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor support zone around the 3,970 level. If we get a pullback, we can expect the buyers to step in around the support, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break to extend the pullback into the minor upward trendline next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Todaywe have the US ADP and the US ISM Services PMI. Tomorrow, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures. On Friday, we conclude the week with the US NFP report and the University of Michigan Consumer sentiment survey.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macro pulse: What if good news for stocks turns into bad news for the bond market?
item.description:
Here's a funny thought. What if the very thing that saves Wall Street from another beating ends up being the thing that sends Treasury yields soaring again? I know, that sounds rather convoluted but hear me out.

Think back to the last two weeks, where we have seen Treasuries enjoy a decent bid lately as investors seek shelter from the growing concerns surrounding AI spending, credit risks, and now the political fallout from the US midterm elections. 10-year yields have fallen back to near 4.90% and have stuck around there since.

Then now, we start to see a Democratic sweep take hold and that puts the focus back on tech stocks once again. The anti-AI and anti-data centre campaigning that helped shape the midterms is now taking over as the one of the core messages from the election results. At first glance, that looks to be quite a headache for tech stocks, no? I mean, slower infrastructure expansion will serve to threaten the growth projections that investors have been banking on.

That being said, what if a little restraint is exactly what the AI trade needs?

After months of investors questioning whether big tech are spending too much and too quickly, perhaps a more measured approach could actually be welcomed. That means less aggressive capital expenditure, which in turn would mean less pressure on borrowing and cash flows. And perhaps more importantly, it will get investors to stop pining over the uncomfortable question of when all that AI investment will start paying off.

Of course, there's a fine line between spending discipline and undermining future growth. But if Wall Street eventually sees the former rather than the latter, equities could find some bit-part relief from the midterms.

If so, a recovery in risk appetite would take away some of the safe-haven demand supporting Treasuries amid heightened AI credit risks in the past few weeks. And that could potentially allow yields to refocus on the inflation pressures and fiscal concerns that have dominated much of the past two months.

However, there is a caveat to all this. And that is Trump decides on what he wants to do with the war against Iran.

After suffering a humiliating defeat in the midterms, Trump now faces the awkward reality that his presidency is going to be one that is defined by the war. So, does he seek an exit or will he double down to avoid looking weak after getting his ego bruised?

Well, I wouldn't dismiss the possibility of the latter - even if a more hostile Congress complicates his options.

Taking that into consideration, another escalation could send oil prices higher and in turn revive inflation fears while pushing Treasury yields back up despite the geopolitical uncertainty.

As such, I would argue that the key for the next move in Treasury yields will come from fading safe-haven demand or renewed inflation fears. But either way, I wouldn't be too quick to assume that the latest rally in the bond market has much further to run. That unless Trump decides to concede and pull back from the Middle East. Now, wouldn't that be something?

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What are the main events for today?
item.description:
EUROPEAN SESSION

In the European session, we get the final services PMI for the major Eurozone economies and the UK. The data won't change anything for the respective central banks, so the market reaction will likely be muted.

The main highlight is going to be the Eurozone CPI report. Headline CPI Y/Y is expected at 4.0% vs 3.8% prior, while the Core CPI Y/Y is seen unchanged at 2.5%. The ECB has signalled that it's ready to hike again if the inflation outlook were to deteriorate and the markets are already pricing in a 72% chance of such a move in December. 

Anyway, the focus should be on the US midterm election results which have seen the Democrats taking control of both the House and the Senate. Although this doesn't take away Trump's power to impose tariffs or continuing the Iran war, it's going to restrict fiscal expansion. 

There's also a risk that Trump decides to escalate the war now that the election has passed, so that's going to be something to keep a close eye on. 

AMERICAN SESSION

In the American session, we have the US ADP and the US ISM Services PMI. The ADP is expected at 67K vs 90K prior, but the data is unlikely to be market-moving given the totality of the data pointing to stable labour market conditions. 

The ISM Services PMI is expected at 54.8 vs 54.9 prior. The S&P Global US Flash Services PMI fell to 57.9 vs 58.8 prior, a two-month low. Nevertheless, the agency said that October's data indicate that the US economy continues to boom at the start of the fourth quarter. If the reopening of the economy after COVID is excluded, recent months have seen the best growth for US businesses since early 2015.

Cost pressures remain a key concern, notably as the renewed surge in oil prices reverberates through to impact a wide variety of goods and services. Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers. The result is the sharpest increase in selling prices for over four years to a pace that indicates consumer price inflation is likely to rise further above the Fed’s target in the coming months.

CENTRAL BANK SPEAKERS

  • 13:20 GMT/08:20 ET - ECB's Lane (neutral - voter)
This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: FX option expiries for 4 November 10am New York cut
item.description:
There are a few key expiry levels to take note of on the day, as highlighted in bold below.

The first one is for EUR/USD at the 1.1250 level, with the strike currently keeping within 30 pips of the spot price. Amid the US midterm election results, we are seeing the dollar soften across the board and that has allowed EUR/USD to come up for some air above the 1.1200 mark.

So, that opens up a bit of room for buyers to work with but there is still some key resistance from the 23.6 Fib retracement level of the swing lower from August to October at 1.1254. As such, the expiries above will add another layer to the resistance point in making it tougher for buyers to try and break away to the upside.

If anything, the expiries will play a small part in anchoring price action closer to 1.1250 on any upside extensions. That being said, dollar sentiment will remain the number one driver as traders continue to digest what to make of Democrats set to take over both the Senate and the House after the midterms. All eyes will be on broader risk sentiment and also what happens to the US-Iran war too after this.

Besides that, there are two key expiries for EUR/GBP at the 0.8330 and 0.8375 levels too. The former is the closer one, seen just 10 pips away from the spot price, and will arguably be the more relevant one. If anything, the expiries will help to act as a bit of a magnet or provide some attraction in keeping any downside extensions in EUR/GBP from running too far in the session ahead.

With all eyes on the dollar right now, the impact of the expiries in EUR/GBP may be relevant amid a lack of other key drivers to influence price action today.

item.title: US futures continue to trim losses after early beatdown but AI worries linger
item.description:
As we look to the session ahead, it seems that Wall Street has finally decided to pick itself up off the floor. But after the beating earlier today, I wouldn't be rushing to vindicate this bounce and label it as a comeback just yet.

US futures are continuing to trim losses with S&P 500 futures now down just 0.3% and Nasdaq futures lower by 0.4%. That's quite the turnaround from earlier in the day when Nasdaq futures were down by over 2% at one point.

The initial selloff came as investors digested the US midterm election results, with the Democratic sweep raising concerns over tougher scrutiny of AI infrastructure spending and data centre development. As such, that puts Wall Street in a bit of an awkward debate right now.

In the past couple of months, investors have been questioning whether big tech is throwing too much money at AI infrastructure without enough to show for it. The astronomical spending commitments have been difficult to justify, especially when the returns remain something of a guessing game for the most part.

Now, wouldn't a slowdown in AI spending actually be a good thing then? Well, yes and no I would say.

On the one hand, tighter spending discipline could be just what investors have been asking for. That means less aggressive capex being deployed and that would in turn ease pressure on cash flows and force tech firms to actually walk the talk. In other words, it will get them to demonstrate that their AI investments can actually generate meaningful returns.

But then, here's the catch. There's a big difference between slowing down on spending voluntarily and being forced to slow down simply because of regulatory hurdles.

If it is more of the latter and we start to see restrictions on data centre development start delaying projects, then that could leave AI companies struggling to secure enough computing capacity to meet growing demand. And with much of the tech sector's growth expectations riding on the AI investment boom, that presents another problem altogether.

If spending plans are scaled back, that could also lead to chipmakers, equipment suppliers and data centre operators facing weaker orders and slower revenue growth in the bigger picture.

In other words, Wall Street might get the spending restraint that it wants so badly before this but perhaps not in the way it had hoped for.

At least for the time being, the recovery in US futures remains tentative at best. If anything, I would be watching whether semiconductor stocks and the broader AI infrastructure trade can find some stability when we get to the Wall Street open later in the day.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US midterms 2026: Who would've thought that a war would be a bad idea?
item.description:
Well, well, well. Who would've thought that starting a war might not be the greatest way to win over voters? That especially when ordinary Americans are the ones feeling the pinch and getting hit where it hurts most, that being their wallets. And now, it looks like Trump is the one paying the political price for his own decisions.

The US midterm election results are delivering a rather profound reality check for Trump, with Democrats riding a blue wave that sees them already take over control of the Senate and closing in on the House. The victories are particularly striking in traditional Republican strongholds, with Democrats flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, and Ohio.

If you're unfamiliar with the political signals, here is the simple breakdown.

Trump isn't losing the presidency today. He will still have two more years left at the helm. However, he will be losing the friendly Congress that helped him push through his agenda for the past two years. And once the Democrats take the House too, the next two years could become a rather frustrating exercise in political gridlock.

So, what exactly went wrong for Trump?

After trying to start a global trade and tariffs war, he was already in a rather unpopular spot. But I'm sure that the real kicker for many is the US-Iran war, and that tipped things over the edge.

Exit polls have shown that most voters believe the US made the wrong decision to attack Iran, while the resulting pressure on energy prices has hardly helped households already struggling with living costs. I mean, voters were already unhappy about the economy and the conflict just added another layer of frustration to that.

As such, what happens in the Middle East now will arguably be the most crucial thing to watch. With Trump already being embarassed back home, will he double down on his aggressive approach and go all guns blazing? Or will Congress be able to call things back and push for a more peaceful transition? That will be the next major thing to watch out for, especially for oil prices and bond yields.

As for Wall Street, the election story is focused elsewhere for now. That being on the growing backlash against AI and data centres.

Opposition to data centre construction emerged as a campaign issue as voters have become more and more concerned about things like electricity costs, infrastructure demands and AI's broader impact on society.

For tech investors, that raises some rather uncomfortable questions about whether the massive AI infrastructure spending boom might run into greater political resistance. And the timing couldn't be worse with markets already looking rather nervous in recent weeks, questioning whether the big spending can generate returns to satisfy investor concerns. It's a bit convoluted but it feels like a damned if you do, damned if you don't situation now.

Nasdaq futures are down 0.7% currently, after having been lower by more than 2% earlier in the day. The bounce is encouraging but I wouldn't read too much into it just yet.

Between political uncertainty, AI spending concerns and the possibility of tighter scrutiny on data centre expansion, tech shares remain the obvious pressure point at this juncture.  I'll keep my eyes on that first but in the grand scheme of things, how things play out with the Iran war is what will be key for broader markets.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Summary:

  • US stock index futures fell as Democrats led the midterm count in both chambers, with S&P 500 e-minis around 7,510 and Nasdaq futures around 27,710
  • AI-linked stocks led Asian losses on fears of tougher US scrutiny of data centres: the Nikkei fell 4.4%, the Kospi 3.3% and the Kosdaq 2.5%
  • Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed four tankers were destroyed by mines south of Hormuz and a US MQ-9 drone was shot down. Neither claim is confirmed
  • Brent traded around $103 and WTI around $96, as Iran-US talks remained stalled
  • New Zealand unemployment rose to 5.7%, an 11-year high, denting the case for a December RBNZ hike
  • China stepped up stock support and moved to slow the yuan’s rally, while Shanghai and Hong Kong edged lower
  • BMW issued a second profit warning, Canada reported progress in US trade talks, and central bank gold buying jumped

US midterms drive risk-off move

Asian markets fell sharply on Wednesday as early results from the US midterm elections showed Democrats ahead in races for both the House and the Senate, prompting investors to dump AI-related stocks. No chamber had been formally called by late in the Asian session.

S&P 500 e-mini futures traded around 7,510 and Nasdaq futures around 27,710, with technology bearing the brunt of the selling. Traders are pricing in more friction for AI and data centre investment, along with the prospect of gridlock and drawn-out bargaining over the debt ceiling and fiscal policy if Democrats take control of Congress.

AI infrastructure became a campaign issue. The Wall Street Journal reported that voter opposition to data centres is strikingly bipartisan, though Democratic candidates have tended to be more sceptical of AI. Democratic candidates for governor in Georgia, Texas and Michigan have called for temporary bans on new data centre construction.

Japan was hit hardest in Asia, retruning from a Tuesday holiday. The Nikkei fell 4.4%, deepening losses through the session as chip equipment maker Advantest, memory chip maker Kioxia, SoftBank Group and fibre-optic cable makers came under heavy selling. South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.3% and the Kosdaq 2.5%, reflecting the market’s heavy exposure to AI chips.

The selling overshadowed strong results overnight from AMD and Super Micro Computer, both of which beat forecasts and guided higher on AI demand.

Iran tensions and oil

Brent crude traded around $103 a barrel and WTI around $96, as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz intensified.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said four tankers had been destroyed and were still burning after striking naval mines south of the strait, and that two other vessels had been detained. Later, it claimed to have shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, which it said was the 56th of its kind. Neither claim had been independently confirmed.

The claims came as a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran and the United States remain far from a deal to end their war. Tehran says the strait will stay closed until Washington waives oil sanctions, ends its naval blockade and releases frozen funds. Qatari mediators said feedback from both sides was expected within 36 hours. President Donald Trump said the US was ready to act but might have no reason to, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has hinted at an attack this week.

The US also updated its security alert for Saudi Arabia, warning of possible Houthi attacks on airports and critical infrastructure and restricting staff travel to areas including the Qatif oil region and the Yanbu export hub.

New Zealand jobs miss

New Zealand’s unemployment rate rose to 5.7% in the third quarter, an 11-year high, against forecasts of 5.5%. Employment fell 0.1% and wage growth slowed to 2.0% a year. The data weakened the case for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to resume rate hikes in December after its surprise hold last week, and two-year swap rates fell. NZD/USD traded around 0.560 ahead of Saturday’s general election. AUD/USD was around 0.696.

China support measures

Chinese markets were little changed, with the Shanghai Composite down 0.1% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng down 0.2%. The People’s Bank of China said applications for its share buyback loan scheme had topped 200bn yuan, after it cut the scheme’s rate to 1% and made it permanent following the CSI 300’s worst month in a decade. The central bank also moved to slow the yuan’s rally, raising banks’ foreign currency reserve requirement and setting a much weaker than expected fixing, which pushed the yuan to a two-week low. A private survey showed services activity growth slowed to a three-month low in October.

Also in focus

BMW issued its second profit warning of the year, cutting its 2026 automotive margin forecast to between minus 0.5% and plus 0.5%, citing faster job cuts, extra production costs and weak demand in China. Its third-quarter results are due on Wednesday.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade talks with the US would intensify, with some red lines removed and Washington asking for less and offering more, though important areas remain unresolved.

The World Gold Council said central bank gold purchases rose 42% in the third quarter, offsetting a slump in jewellery demand. It expects India’s demand to fall to a six-year low in 2026, as high prices and a weak monsoon hit buyers.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China’s yuan slides to two-week low as PBOC moves to slow its rally
item.description:
The PBOC’s moves draw a clear line under how fast it will let the yuan strengthen, which may cap further gains against the dollar and the trade-weighted basket in the near term. A softer yuan could weigh modestly on regional currencies that track it, including the Australian dollar and Korean won, at a time when risk appetite is already fragile because of the US midterms and the Gulf. The step eases pressure on Chinese exporters, which supports the broader effort to stabilise growth and equities alongside this week’s buyback lending measures. The central bank has signalled it has more tools available, so traders may hesitate to bet aggressively on renewed yuan strength.

---

Beijing has decided the yuan has risen far enough for now, and it used both a rule change and its daily fixing to say so.

Summary:

  • The onshore yuan fell to around 6.68 per dollar, its weakest since 19 October, and the offshore yuan slipped about 0.1%
  • The PBOC raised the foreign exchange reserve requirement ratio to 6% from 4% on Tuesday
  • The move is seen as one of its strongest attempts to slow a yuan rally of about 5% this year
  • The PBOC set Wednesday’s midpoint near 6.72, much weaker than the roughly 6.68 expected
  • The CFETS trade-weighted index eased from a 52-month high but is still up about 5.9% this year

China’s yuan fell to its weakest level in more than two weeks against the dollar on Wednesday, Reuters reported. The central bank set a much weaker than expected daily fixing, and investors were digesting its decision to raise banks’ foreign currency reserve requirements.

The onshore yuan weakened to around 6.68 per dollar in morning trade, its softest since 19 October, while the offshore yuan slipped about 0.1% to a similar level.

The move follows the People’s Bank of China’s announcement on Tuesday that it would raise the foreign exchange reserve requirement ratio by 2 percentage points, to 6% from 4%. The ratio sets how much of their foreign currency deposits banks must hold in reserve rather than lend or trade. Raising it reduces the supply of dollars circulating in the onshore market, which tends to support the dollar against the yuan. Traders and analysts described the step as one of the strongest attempts yet to slow the yuan’s rally, which has lifted the currency about 5% against the dollar this year.

A strategist at a European bank told Reuters the central bank was effectively applying the brakes to a surging currency. She said strong Chinese trade was keeping the yuan firm, and that Beijing had plenty of scope to intervene again if the currency’s trade-weighted value kept climbing.

The PBOC reinforced the message on Wednesday with its daily midpoint fixing. It set the midpoint at around 6.72 per dollar, its weakest since 23 October and well below the roughly 6.68 that markets had expected. The spot yuan can trade up to 2% either side of that midpoint each day. Market watchers said the central bank has been guiding the yuan gradually stronger this year, but more slowly than markets anticipated, in an effort to manage the speed of appreciation.

The CFETS index, which tracks the yuan against a basket of trading partners’ currencies, eased to around 103.8 based on Wednesday’s fixing. That was down from a 52-month high on Tuesday, but still up about 5.9% this year, according to Reuters calculations.

The intervention signals that Beijing is wary of a currency strong enough to hurt exporters, at a time when the economy is already contending with weak domestic demand and falling prices.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran’s IRGC says four tankers destroyed by mines south of Hormuz, two vessels detained
item.description:
The claim cuts directly against the early dip in crude, shifting attention from diplomacy and the US midterms back to physical supply risk in the Gulf. Mining is a more serious threat to shipping than isolated attacks, because it puts every vessel in an area at risk and is slow to clear. That would push up tanker freight rates and war-risk insurance premiums, and could prompt more operators to avoid the region. If confirmed, the incident is likely to add a renewed risk premium to Brent and support energy stocks, while weighing on broader risk sentiment already under pressure from the midterm results. It also complicates the Qatari-mediated talks, raising the chance of a wider confrontation involving the US.

---

Earlier:

  • Update: Iran says Hormuz stays shut until demands met as US deal remains far off

--- If the IRGC’s claim holds, the Hormuz stand-off has moved from blockades and talks to mines and burning tankers, and oil’s brief relief may already be over.

Summary:

  • Iran’s IRGC said four tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines south of the Strait of Hormuz
  • It said the tankers were still burning and that two other vessels had been detained
  • The vessels, their flags, cargoes and exact location were not identified
  • There was no immediate independent confirmation
  • The claim comes as Qatar awaits US and Iranian feedback on a possible deal, and hours after limited US strikes on Qeshm island
  • Oil had slipped in early Asian trade before the statement

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said four tankers had been destroyed after striking naval mines south of the Strait of Hormuz, and that two other vessels had been detained. If confirmed, the incident would mark a sharp escalation in the conflict around the world’s most important oil shipping route.

The Guards said the four tankers were still burning. The statement did not identify the vessels, their owners or flags, the cargoes they were carrying or the exact location of the incidents. There was no immediate independent confirmation of the claims. It was also not clear whether there were casualties, or why the two other vessels had been detained.

The claim comes at a delicate moment for diplomacy. A senior Iranian official told Reuters earlier on Tuesday that Iran and the United States remain far apart on a deal to end their war. Tehran insists the strait will stay closed until Washington waives oil sanctions, ends its naval blockade of Iranian ports and releases frozen funds. Qatari mediators said both sides were reviewing proposals, with feedback expected within 36 hours.

Hours earlier, US forces carried out what a US official described as limited, defensive strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island, which sits in the strait, targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets. President Donald Trump said the US was ready to act if needed but might have no reason to, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has hinted at an attack later this week.

The use of naval mines, if confirmed, would raise the stakes for shipping well beyond direct attacks on individual vessels. Mines are difficult to detect and clear, and can threaten any ship passing through an area. That would deter traffic and push up insurance costs, even for tankers with no link to the conflict.

Oil had slipped in early Asian trade on Wednesday as investors looked to the US midterm results and the prospects for talks. The IRGC claim is likely to shift that focus back toward physical supply risk.

Independent confirmation from shipping authorities, maritime security agencies or the vessels’ operators will be key to judging the scale of the incident. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump allies are pointing to the Iran war as the reason for the election disaster
item.description:
The joke tonight is that Trump went to Iran for regime change and he got it, only in the USA.

The numbers so far are ghastly for Republicans in a huge blue wave, including multiple major upsets and a possible Senate majority so large it will be nearly impossible to reverse for 4-6 years.

There is still plenty of counting to do but the blame game has already started and the loudest voices are pointing to a singular target: Iran. If you tune into Fox News, that's what they're talking about. Yes, the "Iran can't get nuclear weapons" talking points continue but it's widely seen as a misstep.

The WSJ is now floating the same thing with "people close to President Trump" blaming the Iran war.

"Some White House officials and Republican allies said the Iran war was misguided, and the midterm elections would have looked very different if the conflict wrapped up months ago."

I tend to agree but that doesn't matter.

What matters is what comes next. This is a key line from the WSJ post:

Trump is also being told by some inside and outside advisers that his legacy will be forever intertwined with the war he launched alongside Israel in February.

That scares me because he might see that as a reason to double down. He could escalate in the hopes of ultimately achieving a win. He could then say that history would judge him kindly.

Alternatively, he could try to wrap it up and spend the next two years working to build his legacy elsewhere, perhaps with an overthrow of Cuba's government or via other endeavors (perhaps a Whtie House ballroom). 

I also think Congress has a role to play here. If the thinking is that the war cost Republicans badly, then they will be motivated to end it as soon as possible. Campaigning on an ongoing war two years from now risks being even more disasterous than tonight, with all three branches of government lost. One candidate to take the falls is Pete Hegseth and the odds of him being replaced are high, if not he could be impeached.

In any case, the Iran file is going to be the thing to watch in the days ahead, especially after today's report that the window to attack again is short.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US futures slide as Democrats lead midterm count, AI data centre fears hit tech
item.description:
Nasdaq futures underperforming the S&P 500 points to a sector story, not just a broad political discount: the market is singling out AI infrastructure as the area most exposed to a shift in Washington. That puts chipmakers, hyperscalers, data centre developers and power and cable suppliers in focus at the cash open. State-level results may matter as much as Congress for these names, given proposed construction bans in key data centre states. The fiscal angle adds a second layer, as renewed debt ceiling brinkmanship could lift volatility and weigh on the dollar if markets price a more fractious 2027. Treasuries may find support as a haven if risk aversion broadens.

-

The midterm count has turned data centres into a market-moving political issue, and tech is bearing the brunt as traders price a Washington less friendly to the AI build-out.

Summary:

  • S&P 500 e-mini futures fell about 1.2% on Globex, with Nasdaq futures down further
  • Early tallies showed Democrats leading 139 to 89 in the House and 46 to 36 in the Senate, with many races uncalled
  • Traders are pricing more friction for AI and data centre investment, plus debt ceiling and fiscal gridlock
  • The Wall Street Journal reported bipartisan voter opposition to data centres, with Democrats generally more AI-sceptical
  • Democratic candidates for governor in Georgia, Texas and Michigan have called for temporary bans on new data centres
  • The selling has already spread to Japan, where the Nikkei fell more than 3%

US stock index futures extended losses as early midterm results showed Democrats ahead in races for both chambers of Congress. Traders are focusing on what a Democratic-controlled Congress could mean for the AI data centre boom and for US fiscal policy.

S&P 500 e-mini futures were down about 1.2% on Globex, with Nasdaq futures falling further as technology stocks bore the brunt of the selling. Early tallies showed Democrats winning 139 House seats to 89 for Republicans, with 218 needed for a majority and many races still to be called. In the Senate, Democrats held 46 seats to 36 for Republicans, a count that includes senators not up for election this year, with 18 seats yet to be decided.

The market reaction is being framed as a classic risk-off move. Traders are pricing in more friction around AI and data centre investment, alongside the prospect of gridlock and drawn-out bargaining over the debt ceiling and fiscal policy, if Democrats take control of Congress while the White House remains Republican.

AI infrastructure has become a political issue in this campaign. The Wall Street Journal reported that opposition to data centres is strikingly bipartisan among voters, though Democratic candidates in national races have tended to be more sceptical of AI than Republicans. In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has criticised tax incentives for technology companies, and called for more transparency, accountability and community input on data centre projects.

The Journal noted that the most significant outcomes for the sector may come at state level. Democratic candidates for governor in Georgia and Texas, two of the busiest states for data centre development, have called for temporary bans on building new server farms. Michigan’s Democratic candidate, Jocelyn Benson, has made a similar proposal.

The selling has already spread to Asia, where Japan’s Nikkei fell more than 3% as investors dumped AI-linked shares, including SoftBank, Advantest and Kioxia.

With many races still uncalled, the final balance of power in both chambers, and the results of key governor contests, will decide whether the pressure on AI-exposed stocks deepens when US cash markets open.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nikkei drops 3% as Democratic midterm gains hit AI and chip stocks
item.description:
The sell-off shows US political risk being priced directly into the AI supply chain, with Japan’s chip equipment, memory and cable makers treated as proxies for US data centre spending. The narrow breadth suggests a targeted rotation out of AI exposure rather than a broad flight from Japanese equities, which may limit wider damage if the US cash session stabilises. Other AI-heavy Asian markets, notably South Korea and Taiwan, are exposed to the same theme. A softer Nikkei could also weigh on sentiment in the yen and Japanese government bonds if risk aversion broadens. Confirmation of the final balance of power in Congress is the key catalyst for whether the move extends.

---

  • Sell tech, sell USD and other signals from the massive blue wave that's unfolding
  • It's no longer early, this election is looking like a disaster for Republicans

---

Tokyo’s AI darlings took the hit for Washington’s shifting balance of power, as investors bet a Democratic Congress means a tougher road for data centre spending.

Summary:

  • The Nikkei fell 3.1% to around 61,130 and the Topix about 1.9% to around 3,860 by 0150 GMT
  • AI-linked stocks led losses on fears of stricter US rules for data centre projects
  • SoftBank fell about 7%, Advantest 6.4%, Tokyo Electron 5% and Kioxia 10%
  • Fibre-optic cable makers Fujikura and Furukawa Electric fell 8.2% and 9%
  • Breadth was mixed, with 130 Nikkei stocks falling and 95 rising
  • Prediction markets pointed to a possible Democratic sweep of Congress, though no chamber has been called

Japan’s Nikkei share average fell more than 3% on Wednesday as AI-related stocks slumped, Reuters reported. Investors were concerned that Democratic gains in the US midterm elections could bring tighter rules for data centre projects and slow spending on AI infrastructure.

The Nikkei was down 3.1% at around 61,130 by 0150 GMT, while the broader Topix index fell about 1.9% to around 3,860. The bigger drop in the Nikkei reflects its heavier weighting toward the large technology and chip stocks that led the decline.

Chip-related shares took the brunt of the selling. Chip-testing equipment maker Advantest fell 6.4% and Tokyo Electron dropped 5%, while technology investor SoftBank Group lost about 7%. Memory chip maker Kioxia slumped 10%. The selling also spread to suppliers of the physical infrastructure behind data centres, with fibre-optic cable makers Fujikura and Furukawa Electric down 8.2% and 9% respectively.

A portfolio manager at a Tokyo-based asset manager told Reuters that Democratic wins in some key states had fuelled caution about stricter regulation of AI infrastructure investment.

The losses were concentrated rather than broad. Of the 225 stocks in the Nikkei, 130 fell and 95 rose, suggesting investors were targeting AI-exposed names rather than selling Japanese equities across the board.

Prediction markets have signalled growing expectations of a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress, with nearly $1.5bn wagered on the elections, Reuters reported. No chamber has yet been formally called. Beyond AI, the result could affect the US fiscal outlook, defence spending and regulation of healthcare, banking and cryptocurrencies.

The sell-off highlights how closely Japan’s market has become tied to the global AI trade, which has driven much of the Nikkei’s rise. It also follows strong results from US chip and server makers overnight, a reminder that political risk is now competing with earnings as a driver of AI stocks.

Investors will be watching the final US results and the reaction in US cash markets for signs of whether the selling in AI-linked shares deepens or eases. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Update: Iran says Hormuz stays shut until demands met as US deal remains far off
item.description:
For oil, the key detail is that Iran has explicitly tied the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to sanctions relief, the end of the US naval blockade and the release of frozen funds. That makes any supply normalisation dependent on a broad political deal rather than a ceasefire alone. The early dip in crude shows traders are leaning toward diplomacy and away from escalation, but the gap between the two sides limits how much risk premium can come out. The next 36 hours of feedback through Qatar is the near-term catalyst: a constructive response could pressure prices further, while a breakdown, or Israeli action without US backing, would likely send them sharply higher. Iran’s threats against US facilities in Europe add a tail risk beyond the Gulf.

---

Both sides are still talking, but Iran has made clear that the price of reopening Hormuz is sanctions relief, and Washington has yet to pay it.

Summary:

  • A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran and the US remain far from a deal
  • Iran says Hormuz will reopen only if oil sanctions are waived, the US naval blockade ends and frozen funds are released
  • Qatar says both sides are reviewing proposals, with feedback expected within 36 hours
  • Trump said the US is ready to strike but may not need to, and that indirect talks on Iran’s enriched uranium are continuing
  • US forces carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island overnight, described as defensive
  • Oil slipped in early Asian trade despite an unexpected fall in US crude stocks

Iran and the United States remain far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. Tehran insisted the Strait of Hormuz would stay closed until its conditions are met, while President Donald Trump said he was ready for further strikes but in no hurry to launch them.

The official said mediators were working hard to narrow the gaps, but that Iran would not accept what it views as excessive US demands. Tehran’s conditions for reopening Hormuz include the waiving of oil sanctions, an end to the US naval blockade of its ports and the release of frozen Iranian funds. Nuclear talks could begin only once those conditions were met, the official said. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Washington’s response so far had not been convincing, and that the strait would reopen only if the US addressed all seven of Iran’s conditions.

Qatar is leading the mediation. Its foreign ministry said both sides were reviewing proposals, and an official briefed on the talks told Reuters that feedback from Washington and Tehran was expected within 36 hours. A senior Iranian official later said there was no deadline for exchanging messages.

Trump struck a mixed tone in separate interviews. He told the Financial Times that the US appeared to be getting everything it wanted and that, while it was ready to act, there might be no reason to. He said indirect talks on Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium were ongoing. In a Fox News interview, he said he did not want large loss of life but would act if required.

Military activity has not stopped. US forces carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island overnight, targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets. A US official described the strikes as defensive and said they did not signal a return to major combat. Iranian officials warned of an immediate response to any further attack, unconstrained by geography.

Trump also announced a deal with Israel under which the US would end $4bn in annual funding after this year, while continuing to sell it weapons.

Oil prices slipped in early Asian trade on Wednesday, Reuters reported, as investors awaited the midterm results and their implications for the talks. The dip came despite industry data showing an unexpected fall in US crude inventories. 

Back to business tomorrow. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China services PMI slows to 50.8 in October as price cuts meet rising costs
item.description:
The data adds to the picture of a Chinese economy still growing but struggling with weak pricing power, which helps explain why authorities are leaning on targeted support such as this week’s expanded buyback lending. Falling selling prices alongside rising costs point to margin pressure for listed service companies, which may limit any equity bounce from the support measures. Firms specifically cited oil among rising input costs, a sign that higher energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict are filtering into China’s economy even as companies cannot pass them on. For the Australian dollar and commodities, the slightly firmer manufacturing output is a modest offset, but the softer services reading gives little reason to expect a stronger demand impulse from China.

--- Chinese service firms are still finding customers and hiring staff, but they are cutting prices to do it while their own costs climb, a squeeze that shows up in profits before it shows up in growth.

Summary:

  • The RatingDog China General Services PMI fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6, the slowest growth in three months
  • New business rose at a solid pace, and new export orders grew for a sixth month
  • Employment rose for a sixth month at a faster pace, and backlogs fell for the first time in a year, helped by AI efficiencies
  • Selling prices fell for a second month, while input costs rose at the fastest pace in five months on labour, raw material and oil costs
  • Business confidence slipped to a three-month low
  • The composite PMI fell to 52.0 from 52.4, despite faster manufacturing output growth

China’s services sector kept growing in October but at a slower pace, a private survey showed on Wednesday. Firms cut prices to win business even though their own costs rose at the fastest rate in five months.

The RatingDog China General Services PMI, compiled by S&P Global, fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6 in September. The reading stayed above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction, but it showed the slowest growth in activity in three months. Firms pointed to operational constraints as a factor behind the slowdown.

Demand held up better than the headline suggests. New business continued to rise at a solid pace, little changed from September, extending a run of growth that began in January 2023. Firms credited wider customer bases and successful promotional efforts. New export orders rose for a sixth straight month, the longest stretch since 2024, though growth eased and was marginal.

Hiring picked up. Employment rose for a sixth month, and at a faster pace than in September, as firms took on both full- and part-time staff. The extra workers, along with what firms described as efficiency gains from AI, helped reduce backlogs of work for the first time in a year.

Pricing remains the main concern. Average selling prices fell for a second month as firms discounted to cope with fierce competition, although the pace of discounting eased from September. At the same time, input cost inflation hit a five-month high, driven by higher labour, raw material and oil costs, with some firms also citing social security payments. That combination points to pressure on profit margins.

Business confidence stayed positive but slipped to a three-month low, as firms worried about rising costs and competition.

A separate composite index, which combines manufacturing and services, fell to 52.0 from 52.4, the slowest rise in private sector output in three months. Faster growth in manufacturing output was not enough to offset the softer services expansion.

RatingDog founder Yao Yu said that steady new business and stronger hiring underpinned growth at the start of the fourth quarter, but that renewed discounting and rising costs were weighing on profitability. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Sell tech, sell USD and other signals from the massive blue wave that's unfolding
item.description:
The US dollar is selling off as the election results roll in and they show a total repudation of Republican policies.

Fox News is talking about the Iran war as a disaster at the ballot box and in terms of affordability, which was clearly on the ballot. Tariffs aren't far behind. 

Still, it's tough to price in a reversal in Iran or on tariffs with Trump in office for another two years. What is driving markets and could swing is data centers and AI. Democrats took an anti-AI stance or at least something slower than the full-throttle roll out now. In Texas and Ohio in particular, data centers became a huge issue and it looks like the pro-data center candidates will lose the Governorship. 

Moreover, tech companies dove into bed with Trump ahead of the last election and most have gotten more-deeply involved since, as they were given to move fast and break things. Now, Democrats might look for some retribution for the massive checks they wrote to Republicans, via regulation, fines and investigations. That's why the Nasdaq is down 1.5% at the moment.

Moreover, the AI trade is vulnerable already and this could tip it further. In terms of FX, the dollar is increasingly an AI-investment trade. If we see a reversal of the flows into AI, that means the money will flow out of USD. We've seen this dynamic unfolding in the past two months with an increasingly-tight correlation. 

I worry there could be some second and third order effects if Trump attacks Iran in a fit, or grows less predictable. For now, I think the market is sending the right signals: Sell tech, sell USD.

To give you a sense of how big of an upset this is -- even compared to expectations -- is that Lindsay Graham's seat looks lost. The odds of that in October were just 14%.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: China buyback loan applications top 200bn yuan as PBOC steps up stock support
item.description:
The modest early gains suggest the measures are steadying sentiment rather than sparking a rebound, consistent with the scheme’s role as a backstop. The benefit is likely to be greatest for large, cash-rich companies with high dividend yields, such as state-owned banks and energy firms, which can borrow cheaply to buy back shares. The tool does little directly for the tech and AI names behind October’s sell-off, so Hong Kong-listed tech remains exposed to AI earnings concerns. For the Australian dollar and iron ore, stabilising Chinese equities offer marginal support, but property and consumption data remain the bigger drivers.

---

Beijing is not buying stocks itself, but it is making it very cheap for companies and their owners to do so, and demand for that money is climbing fast.

Summary:

  • Applications for the PBOC’s share buyback and stake-increase relending scheme have topped 200bn yuan, about $30bn
  • The PBOC said it has intensified the policy to keep capital markets stable
  • This week it cut the facility rate to 1% from 1.25%, made the tool permanent and widened eligibility
  • A separate 100bn yuan asset swap facility for brokers, fund managers and insurers began on Tuesday
  • The CSI 300 fell 8.5% in October, its worst month in a decade, on doubts over AI and tech spending
  • Shanghai stocks edged higher in early trade

Applications for China’s central bank-backed share buyback loans have topped 200bn yuan, or about $30bn, the People’s Bank of China said on Wednesday, according to Reuters. Authorities are stepping up efforts to steady a stock market that has suffered its worst month in a decade. Mainland shares edged higher in early trade, with the Shanghai Composite up about 0.2% at around 3,610 shortly after the open.

The PBOC said it had intensified its share repurchase and shareholding relending policies to keep capital markets stable. The update follows a meeting on Monday at which the central bank and financial and securities regulators met major banks to discuss how to improve the scheme.

So how does it work? The facility, launched in October 2024 with a quota of 300bn yuan, is a form of targeted cheap funding. Commercial banks lend to listed companies so they can buy back their own shares, and to major shareholders so they can raise their stakes. The PBOC then supplies low-cost funding to the banks to cover those loans, which is what relending means. The central bank does not buy shares itself. Instead, it lowers the cost for companies and their main owners to do so.

The aim is to put a floor under prices. Buybacks reduce the number of shares in circulation and signal that insiders see value at current levels. Because the loans are cheap, a company can borrow to buy its own stock when its dividend yield exceeds the cost of borrowing, which turns falling prices into an incentive to buy.

Authorities made the scheme more generous this week. On Monday, the PBOC cut the interest rate it charges banks under the facility to 1% from 1.25%, made the tool a permanent part of its policy kit and widened the range of eligible companies. It also opened a separate asset swap facility of about 100bn yuan. That facility lets brokers, fund managers and insurers swap assets for more liquid securities, which they can use to raise cash to buy shares.

The push comes after a sharp sell-off. The CSI 300 index of major mainland stocks fell 8.5% in October and entered a bear market on 20 October, hit by doubts over whether Chinese AI and technology companies will earn back their heavy spending. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-linked firms make up about 42% of the market value of Chinese shares listed on the mainland and in Hong Kong.

Tools like this have limits. Buybacks support prices but do not fix the underlying problems weighing on Chinese stocks, including weak consumption and a long property downturn. Repurchased shares that are not cancelled can also be sold back into the market later, and borrowing to buy stock adds to corporate debt. The scheme works best as a backstop that slows selling, rather than as a trigger for a lasting rally. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: It's no longer early, this election is looking like a disaster for Republicans
item.description:
It's no longer early as US votes roll in.

There is a highly statistically significant number of districts reporting now and some of them reporting completely. The numbers are showing a 10-35 point swing towards Democrats. If even the bottom of that holds, it's a huge swing towards Democrats.

For illustration, betting odds now have Democrats winning the Texas Governorship and Senate seat, with Talarico beating Paxton at 95%. In the closely-watched early numbers in KY-06 and IN-05 the numbers are unmistakable and show Democrats upsetting Republicans in both. Florida hasn't been as much of a landslide but it has shown a shift to Democrats of around 10 points from 2024.

Another huge upset brewing is in South Carolina, where Lindsay Graham's sister was running for his seat after his death. Odds now have her narrowly losing the seat, which would hand it to Democrats for the next 6 years.

It seems that all that's left to do is tally the margin of victory.

In terms of markets, I would be careful with tech because anti data-centers was a strong campaign message and anti-AI in general. The tech right got into bed with Trump and now there might be a price to pay. That's particularly notable in Texas, where there are a huge amount of data centers planned. Shares of Tesla are down 3% overnight and I think that's an interesting spot to watch if the Democrat wins the Governorship. 

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stock futures slip on Globex as early midterm results point to Democratic gains
item.description:
The reaction is likely to spill into Asian trade, where regional equities tend to follow US futures in the absence of a local catalyst. The dollar and Treasuries are worth watching for signs of whether markets see a Democratic Congress as reducing fiscal stimulus expectations, which would tend to support bonds. Oil could be sensitive to any shift in expectations for Iran policy, with congressional constraints on military action potentially easing the geopolitical risk premium. Volatility measures may stay elevated until the balance of power in both chambers is confirmed.

---

Earlier:

  • The very early results in Kentucky show a massive swing towards Democrats

---

Futures are trading the early midterm returns before the votes are counted, betting that a divided Washington means less policy support and more political noise.

Summary:

  • US stock index futures traded lower on Globex as early midterm results pointed to Democratic gains
  • No call has yet been made on control of the House or Senate
  • Narratives include a stalled legislative agenda, renewed fiscal standoffs and greater oversight of the administration
  • Technology, pharma, financials, energy and defence could face sector-specific pressure
  • Gridlock has historically been seen as benign for stocks, and markets have often rallied after midterms
  • Thin overnight liquidity means early moves may not last

US stock index futures traded lower on Globex as early results from Tuesday’s midterm elections pointed to Democratic gains. Traders are weighing the prospect that the party could take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

No call has yet been made on the balance of power in either chamber, and counting is continuing. The moves in futures reflect early positioning in thin overnight trade rather than a settled verdict on the result.

Several explanations are circulating for the weakness. The most direct is that a Democratic Congress would end the White House’s ability to pass its agenda through the legislature. Further tax cuts, deregulation and other fiscal measures that some investors had built into earnings expectations would become much harder to deliver.

Divided government would also bring back the risk of standoffs over government funding and the debt ceiling, which have produced bouts of volatility in past cycles. A Democratic House would gain subpoena power and control of committees, raising the prospect of investigations into the administration and adding to political uncertainty.

Some of the pressure may show up at the sector level. Technology and AI companies could face more scrutiny through congressional hearings, drugmakers may see renewed pressure on pricing, and banks and crypto firms may find deregulation slows. Energy and defence stocks could also be sensitive to any congressional effort to limit military action against Iran or to challenge the administration’s tariff powers.

There are reasons for caution about reading too much into the early moves. Market wisdom has long held that gridlock can be positive for stocks because it limits major policy shifts. US equities have also historically tended to perform well in the months after midterm elections, once uncertainty clears. Overnight liquidity is thin, and other factors, including the Iran stand-off and concerns about AI valuations, have weighed on sentiment this week.

The cash market open, and confirmation of control in each chamber, will give a clearer read on whether the selling extends or fades.

Team Trump not having a good evening so far

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Recap: New Zealand jobless rate hits 11-year high, kiwi slips as RBNZ hike bets fade
item.description:
The steady drift lower in the kiwi since the release suggests traders are pricing out some of the chance of a December hike rather than reacting to a one-off headline. The fall in two-year swaps supports that reading. With the RBA still leaning hawkish, the widening policy gap leaves NZD/AUD vulnerable to further weakness. The election is the next risk: a Labour-led win would bring the prospect of a dual mandate, which markets would likely read as tilting the RBNZ toward easier policy over time. Inflation expectations surveys later this month are the next test of whether the RBNZ’s hawks can still make their case.

---

Earlier:

  • NZ Q3 Unemployment rate 5.7% (expected 5.5%, prior 5.6%)

---

New Zealand’s jobs data missed on every measure, handing the RBNZ a reason to stay on hold and the opposition a fresh line of attack days before the vote.

Summary:

  • Unemployment rose to 5.7% in Q3, the highest since 2015, against expectations of 5.5% from both economists and the RBNZ
  • Employment fell 0.1% and participation slipped to 70.4%
  • Private sector wage growth slowed to 0.4% in the quarter and 2.0% on the year
  • The kiwi dipped, steadied around $0.56 and has drifted lower since, while two-year swaps fell about 6bp
  • Labour called the data a verdict on the government, while the finance minister urged voters to stick with its plan
  • Labour has pledged to restore a dual mandate for the RBNZ if elected on Saturday

New Zealand’s unemployment rate climbed to an 11-year high in the third quarter, data released earlier on Wednesday showed. The New Zealand dollar has traded lower since, as markets weigh the outlook for interest rates and Saturday’s general election.

To recap, the jobless rate rose to 5.7% in the three months to September, the highest since 2015, according to Statistics New Zealand. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 5.5%, as had the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Employment fell 0.1% from the previous quarter, against forecasts of a 0.4% rise, and the participation rate slipped to 70.4%, below the 70.7% expected.

Wage growth also slowed. Private sector labour costs excluding overtime rose 0.4% in the quarter, down from 0.7% in the previous three months, taking annual growth to 2.0% from 2.1%.

The figures land in the final days of a tight election campaign, Reuters reported, with an Ipsos poll this week showing inflation and the cost of living as voters’ top concern. Labour’s finance spokesperson, Barbara Edmonds, said the data was a damning judgement on Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s handling of the economy. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the numbers reflected the effect of uncertainty and showed the need to stay with the government’s plan, which she said was rebuilding the economy.

Markets read the data as reducing pressure on the central bank to resume rate rises. The kiwi dipped on the release before steadying around $0.56, Reuters reported, and has since drifted lower. Two-year swap rates fell about 6 basis points to around 3.78%.

The RBNZ surprised markets last week by holding its official cash rate at 2.75%. It said it wanted time to judge the effect of two earlier hikes, while signalling further increases were still likely. Economists at one local bank said the weakening labour market made that decision look increasingly justified, and suggested further hikes may not be needed if the trend continued.

The election adds a further policy question. Labour has pledged to return the RBNZ to a dual mandate covering both price stability and maximum sustainable employment, rather than its current single focus on inflation. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tesla misled South Korean buyers over Full Self-Driving, consumer group alleges
item.description:
The direct financial hit to Tesla is likely small, but the case adds to regulatory and reputational risk around Full Self-Driving, a product central to the company’s valuation story. A cease-and-desist order or fines in a fast-growing market would be a setback. Refund claims would be a bigger issue if they spread to other countries selling China-built cars. The dispute also highlights how much Tesla’s international software revenue depends on certification regimes it does not control, which matters as it pushes for approval in Europe. Investors will watch whether the regulator acts quickly and whether similar complaints emerge elsewhere.

---

Tesla’s South Korean boom was built on China-made cars, and a consumer group says the company sold their owners self-driving software they could never legally switch on.

Summary:

  • A consumer group plans to file a complaint on Thursday alleging Tesla misled South Korean buyers over Full Self-Driving, Reuters reported
  • Only about 20% of Teslas registered in South Korea, those made in the US, can legally use the software
  • 99% of new Teslas sold in South Korea last year were China-made and ineligible
  • Tesla charged about 9 million won (around $6,700) for the software before moving to a monthly subscription in August
  • The group seeks a cease-and-desist order, fines and a referral to state investigators
  • The regulator already opened a probe into Tesla’s advertising earlier this year

A consumer advocacy group alleges that Tesla misled tens of thousands of South Korean customers by marketing its Full Self-Driving software, even though the company knew the software could not legally be used in most of its cars sold there. The group plans to file a complaint on Thursday, Reuters reported.

According to Reuters, which has seen the previously unreported complaint, Citizens United for Consumer Sovereignty will ask the Korea Fair Trade Commission to issue a temporary cease-and-desist order on marketing the software for ineligible vehicles. It will also seek administrative fines and a referral to state investigators. Tesla did not respond to requests for comment.

At the centre of the dispute is where the cars are built. Tesla Korea’s country manager told a parliamentary hearing last month that the software can be used on only about 20% of Tesla vehicles registered in South Korea. Those are the US-built cars, which meet American safety standards recognised under a free trade agreement. Most Teslas sold in the country are made in China, where no such arrangement exists.

Tesla has sold more than 170,000 Shanghai-built vehicles in South Korea since 2023, according to company data submitted to the National Assembly. Last year, 99% of new Teslas sold in the country could not legally use the software. For years, Tesla charged customers a one-off payment of about 9 million won, or roughly $6,700, before switching to a monthly subscription of about 150,000 won in August.

The complaint alleges Tesla promoted the feature as coming soon and released a demonstration video filmed in South Korea, without clearly disclosing that only a small fraction of its cars could use it. The group’s automotive lead said Tesla had earned substantial revenue from selling a costly system that many buyers could not use at all.

Regulatory scrutiny was already under way. A commission official said it opened a probe into Tesla’s advertising of the software earlier this year and has received written responses from the company. The transport ministry has said the software does not meet local safety rules, including a requirement for drivers to keep their hands on the wheel. Tesla applied for certification of China-made vehicles only in late October.

The case comes as Tesla’s sales in South Korea surge. It overtook BMW this year as the country’s top imported car brand.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6811 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
Yesterday the PNoC made moves to slow the yuan appreciation:

  • China’s PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD

---

The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

Pan Gongsheng, Governor of the People's Bank of China

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: India gold demand seen at six-year low in 2026 as high prices and weak monsoon bite
item.description:
Weak Indian buying removes an important source of physical support for gold, leaving prices more reliant on central bank purchases and fund inflows. Lower imports would ease pressure on India’s trade deficit and offer modest support to the rupee, though the reported rise in unofficial inflows means official import data may understate actual demand. The Diwali and wedding season is the near-term test: a muted festival response would confirm that current prices have moved beyond what Indian households will pay. For the wider gold market, it reinforces a pattern of strong official demand alongside a retreat by price-sensitive consumers.

---

Earlier:

  • Central bank gold buying jumps 42% in Q3 as high prices hit jewellery demand, WGC says

---

The world’s second-biggest gold buyer is pulling back, priced out by gold’s rally and squeezed by a failed monsoon, just as its key buying season begins.

Summary:

  • The WGC expects India’s 2026 gold demand to fall to around 650 tons, the lowest since 2020
  • September-quarter demand fell 29% to around 160 tons, with jewellery down 20% and investment down 40%
  • Rising living costs since the Iran war and the weakest monsoon in more than a decade are weighing on rural buying
  • Rural areas account for more than half of India’s gold demand
  • Festival and wedding demand should lift the December quarter, but high prices are expected to cap the recovery
  • Official imports fell partly due to more unofficial inflows after higher import duties

India’s gold demand is expected to fall to a six-year low in 2026, as elevated prices weigh on jewellery buying and investment demand weakens, the World Gold Council said on Tuesday, according to Reuters.

The industry body expects total demand in the world’s second-largest gold consumer to fall to around 650 metric tons this year. That would be the lowest since 2020, when pandemic lockdowns forced jewellery shops to close. Sachin Jain, chief executive of the council’s Indian operations, told Reuters that weaker jewellery sales over the first nine months of the year would drag down the annual total.

Demand fell 29% from a year earlier to around 160 tons in the September quarter, Jain said. Jewellery purchases dropped 20%, while investment demand fell 40%.

The figures show high prices hitting Indian buyers harder than the global market. The council’s global report, also released on Tuesday, showed worldwide demand roughly flat on the year in the third quarter, with strong central bank buying offsetting weaker jewellery and retail investment.

Indian households are also facing rising living costs following the Iran war, and the weather has added to the strain. The 2026 monsoon delivered its lowest rainfall in more than a decade, cutting farm output and incomes in rural areas. Those areas account for more than half of the country’s gold demand, and jewellery there serves as a traditional store of wealth.

Jain said demand should pick up in the December quarter, when festivals and the wedding season typically lift purchases. Diwali, when buying gold is considered auspicious, falls in early November. However, the council said high prices and the weak rural economy were likely to limit any recovery.

India’s official gold imports also fell in the September quarter. Jain attributed part of the decline to a rise in unofficial inflows after the government raised import duties on gold earlier this year. That suggests official data may understate how much gold is entering the country. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The very early results in Kentucky show a massive swing towards Democrats
item.description:
I highlighted KY-06 as an early district to watch as a barometer of today's vote and now some real results are crossing and betting markets are moving.

In Anderson County, the numbers show the Republican Alvarado leading by 19 percentage points. That's good, right? No, it's not because in the prior three House elections, the Republican won that county +48, +54 and +54. So that's around a 35-points swing towards the Democrat candidate with 49% of votes counted.

In Montgomery County on the opposite side of the district, 43% of votes are counted and the patter is similar. It shows Alvarado up 16 points but that compares to +53 in the prior election, +54 in 2022 and +43 in 2020.

In Jessamine County, with 27% of the vote, Dumbo leads +0.9% and that compares to R+46.3% in 2024, a huge swing. That's a smaller percentage of the vote but the raw number is triple the size of the other two counties that have reported.

That looks like a Democratic landslide and prediction markets appear to endorse it. 

There has also been a notable move towards Democrats winning the Senate at 86% compared to 73% earlier today.

For Kentucky, there is an important caveat here. Nearly all Kentucky counties are expected to report early and absentee votes in their first update, according to the Associated Press. Those numbers are likely from early and mail-in voters, which skew Democrat. 

Update: Likely the most-significant data point yet is in. 95% of votes are in for Powell County in KY-06 and that's a 28.7 pt swing to Dems vs 2024 and 27 pts vs 2022. With the high % counted, it can't be a mail-in skew.

Update 2: Now we have 89-92% of votes counted in Montgomery, Anderson and Bourbon Counties. As the later votse come in, we've seen a 3-5 point swing towards the Republicans but that's still a massive underperformance compared to 2024. In those counties, the movement is Dem +32.4, +32.3 and +37.4 points. Dumbo is now pricing at 95%.

If that translates nationally, it will be a LANDSLIDE.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.
